reasons: argparse is in the standard library, so the tool has no dependency to install, pin or upgrade over years of solo maintenance.
Three subcommands are well within argparse's subparsers. The boilerplate is modest and stable.
Python 3.11 is fixed, and argparse's API has been stable across versions. click and typer add third-party release and compatibility churn, and typer also pulls in click.
If the tool outgrows argparse, migrating a small CLI to click or typer later is cheap.
risks: I did not inspect the repo, so I don't know whether it already depends on click or typer. If it does, that would favor reusing it.
argparse needs more boilerplate for subcommands and gives less polished help output than click or typer.
If the subcommands grow complex, with nested groups, shell completion or rich prompts, argparse becomes tedious.
would_change_if: The repo already depends on click or typer, or the CLI is expected to grow well beyond three simple subcommands.
